evidence: This is an inference based on the assumption about recombination and introgression, supported by citations.

claim: A star tree is obtained whenever H. erato is assumed to diverge before H. aoede (scenario 1) under the MSC-with-migration (MSC-M or isolation-with-migration; IM) model of three species.
source: Second, we obtain a star tree whenever H. erato is assumed to diverge before H. aoede (scenario 1) under the MSC-with-migration (MSC-M or isolation-with-migration; IM) model of three species that allows for gene flow between two ingroup species since their divergence but does not allow gene flow with the outgroup species (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-M analysis.

claim: Star trees are commonly observed when the assumed bifurcating tree is incorrect.
source: Star trees are commonly observed when the assumed bifurcating tree is incorrect (Dalquen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Assuming H. aoede diverges before H. erato (scenario 2) always leads to a bifurcating tree under the MSC-M model.
source: By contrast, assuming H. aoede diverges before H. erato (scenario 2) always leads to a bifurcating tree.
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-M analysis.

claim: Four small inversion regions (~100–400 kb) had been identified previously to be differentially fixed between the melpomene group and the erato-sara clade: 2b, 6b, 6c, 13b, and 21b.
source: Four small inversion regions (~100–400 kb) had been identified previously to be differentially fixed between the melpomene group and the erato-sara clade (Seixas et al., 2021): 2b, 6b, 6c, 13b, and 21b.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The 13b region (~360 kb with respect to H. erato demophoon reference) consistently shows a unique pattern in which H. doris and H. burneyi cluster with the erato-sara clade instead of the melpomene-silvaniform clade.
source: While species tree estimates are more uncertain (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Supplementary file 1d–g), the 13b region (~360 kb with respect to H. erato demophoon reference) consistently shows a unique pattern in which H. doris and H. burneyi cluster with the erato-sara clade instead of the melpomene-silvaniform clade.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the 13b inversion region.

claim: The unique pattern in the 13b region suggests ancient introgression of the inversion from the erato-sara clade into H. doris and H. burneyi.
source: This suggests ancient introgression of the inversion from the erato-sara clade into H. doris and H. burneyi (Seixas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic pattern, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Some hitherto unrecognized introgression among the deepest branches within Heliconius sensu lato was detected.
source: In conclusion, we detect some hitherto unrecognized introgression among the deepest branches within Heliconius sensu lato.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis.

claim: The aoede-early scenario coupled with deep introgression events may have led to some of the morphological and ecological evidence previously used in support of the erection the subgenera Neruda (for H. aoede and allies) as well as Laparus (for H. doris) that appeared to conflict with more recent molecular genetic data.
source: The aoede-early scenario coupled with these deep introgression events may have led to some of the morphological and ecological evidence previously used in support of the erection the subgenera Neruda (for H. aoede and allies [Turner, 1976]) as well as Laparus (for H. doris [Turner, 1968]) that appeared to conflict with more recent molecular genetic data.
evidence: This is an inference about how the phylogenetic findings reconcile with prior taxonomic and morphological evidence, with citations.

claim: The melpomene-silvaniform clade is one of the most phylogenetically difficult groups of Heliconius due to ongoing hybridization and extensive gene flow involving most members of the group.
source: This is one of the most phylogenetically difficult groups of Heliconius due to ongoing hybridization and extensive gene flow involving most members of the group (Mallet et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a characterization of the group with a citation.

claim: Previous studies have inferred conflicting introgression scenarios in the melpomene-silvaniform clade.
source: Previous studies have inferred conflicting introgression scenarios in this clade (Martin et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016; Jay et al., 2018; Edelman et al., 2019; Cicconardi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The analysis confirms widespread introgression within the melpomene-silvaniform clade.
source: Our analysis below confirms widespread introgression within this clade.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analysis.

claim: Four major species relationships were identified from blockwise estimates of species trees under the MSC model without gene flow: (a) autosome-majority (trees 1–3), (b) autosome-variant (trees 5–7), (c) the Z chromosome (chr. 21; tree 4), and (d) chromosome 15 inversion region (15b; tree 24).
source: We identify four major species relationships from blockwise estimates of species trees under the MSC model without gene flow (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1m and n): (a) autosome-majority (trees 1–3), (b) autosome-variant (trees 5–7), (c) the Z chromosome (chr. 21; tree 4), and (d) chromosome 15 inversion region (15b; tree 24).
evidence: This is a finding from the blockwise species tree analysis.

claim: The pattern of four major species relationships is highly similar between coding and noncoding loci.
source: The pattern is highly similar between coding and noncoding loci.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing coding and noncoding data.

claim: The first three relationships (trees 1–9) account for >90% of the blocks, with a well-supported pardalinus-hecale clade ((H. pardalinus, H. elevatus), H. hecale) and a cydno-melpomene clade ((H. timareta, H. cydno), H. melpomene).
source: The first three relationships (trees 1–9) account for >90% of the blocks, with a well-supported pardalinus-hecale clade ((H. pardalinus, H. elevatus), H. hecale) and a cydno-melpomene clade ((H. timareta, H. cydno), H. melpomene).
evidence: This is a finding from the blockwise species tree analysis.

claim: The Z-chromosome tree (tree 4 in scenario c) is the MAP tree with a high posterior probability in almost all blocks of the Z chromosome (median probability of 1).
source: The Z-chromosome tree (i.e. tree 4 in scenario c) is the MAP tree with a high posterior probability in almost all blocks of the Z chromosome (median probability of 1; Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1m), with H. besckei + H. numata diverging first, followed by a split between the pardalinus-hecale clade and the cydno-melpomene clade.
evidence: This is a finding from the Z chromosome analysis.

claim: A similar distinction between the autosome-majority trees and the Z-chromosome tree was also found by Zhang et al., 2016.
source: A similar distinction between the autosome-majority trees and the Z-chromosome tree was also found by Zhang et al., 2016.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: All four scenarios a–d confirm paraphyly of the silvaniform species (H. besckei, H. numata, and the pardalinus-hecale clade), consistent with some recent phylogenomic studies.
source: All four scenarios a–d confirm paraphyly of the silvaniform species (H. besckei, H. numata, and the pardalinus-hecale clade), consistent with some recent phylogenomic studies (Zhang et al., 2016; Massardo et al., 2020; Cicconardi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a phylogenetic finding supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Monophyly of the silvaniforms was suggested in concatenation/sliding-window analysis, but this conclusion may suffer from a failure to account for deep coalescence.
source: Monophyly of the silvaniforms was suggested in concatenation/sliding-window analysis (Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Kozak et al., 2015; Kozak et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021), but this conclusion may suffer from a failure to account for deep coalescence (Edwards et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work with citations.

claim: Substantial introgression from the pardalinus-hecale + cydno-melpomene clade into H. numata was found on the autosomes, and to a lesser extent, between H. numata and the pardalinus-hecale clade.
source: On the autosomes, there is substantial introgression from the pardalinus-hecale + cydno-melpomene clade into H. numata, and to a lesser extent, between H. numata and the pardalinus-hecale clade.
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-I analysis.

claim: These patterns match well with the frequencies of the two main autosomal relationships (scenarios a and b).
source: These patterns match well with the frequencies of the two main autosomal relationships (scenarios a and b in Figure 2).
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency between introgression patterns and tree frequencies.

claim: Within the cydno-melpomene clade, introgression is predominantly unidirectional from H. cydno and H. timareta into H. melpomene.
source: Within the cydno-melpomene clade, introgression is predominantly unidirectional from H. cydno and H. timareta into H. melpomene.
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-I analysis.

claim: The H. pardalinus–H. elevatus pair shows ongoing extensive but variable introgression across the genome, with the introgression time estimated to be zero.
source: The H. pardalinus–H. elevatus pair shows ongoing extensive but variable introgression across the genome, with the introgression time estimated to be zero.
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-I analysis.

claim: The age of the melpomene-silvaniform clade (τr) is estimated to be ~0.020 substitutions per site based on noncoding data.
source: The age of the melpomene-silvaniform clade (τr) is estimated to be ~0.020 substitutions per site based on noncoding data (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, Supplementary file 1q).
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the MSC-I analysis.

claim: The age of the melpomene-silvaniform clade translates to ~1.7 (CI: 0.9, 3.8) million years ago (Ma), assuming a neutral mutation rate of 2.9 × 10–9 per site per generation (95% CI: 1.3 × 10–9, 5.5 × 10–9) and four generations per year.
source: This translates to ~1.7 (CI: 0.9, 3.8) million years ago (Ma), assuming a neutral mutation rate of 2.9 × 10–9 per site per generation (95% CI: 1.3 × 10–9, 5.5 × 10–9) and four generations per year (Keightley et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conversion of the divergence time estimate to absolute time using a mutation rate from the literature.

claim: The age estimate is not very different from a previous estimate of 3.7 (CI: 3.2, 4.3) Ma based on molecular clock dating, which ignores ancestral polymorphism and is therefore expected to overestimate divergence time.
source: This is not very different from a previous estimate of 3.7 (CI: 3.2, 4.3) Ma based on molecular clock dating (Kozak et al., 2015), which ignores ancestral polymorphism and is therefore expected to overestimate divergence time.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work and an explanation of why the prior estimate might be biased.

claim: Estimates of species divergence time tend to be precise and highly similar across the genome.
source: Overall, our estimates of species divergence time tend to be precise and highly similar across the genome (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of parameter estimates.

claim: The posterior means from coding and noncoding loci are strongly correlated, with τC ≈ bτNC where b varies between 0.4 and 0.6 (r2 > 0.95) in most chromosomal regions.
source: The posterior means from coding and noncoding loci are strongly correlated, with τC ≈ bτNC where b varies between 0.4 and 0.6 (r2 > 0.95) in most chromosomal regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between coding and noncoding estimates.

claim: The scale factor of b < 1 can be explained by purifying selection removing deleterious nonsynonymous mutations in coding regions of the genome.
source: The scale factor of b < 1 can be explained by purifying selection removing deleterious nonsynonymous mutations in coding regions of the genome (Shi and Yang, 2018).
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed pattern with a citation.

claim: Present-day and ancestral population sizes (θ) are of the order of 0.01.
source: Present-day and ancestral population sizes (θ) are of the order of 0.01 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, Supplementary file 1q and r).
evidence: This is a parameter estimate from the analysis.

claim: For inbred individuals among the genomic data (H. melpomene, H. timareta, H. numata, and H. pardalinus), θ estimates vary among chromosomes by orders of magnitude, with the inbred genome of H. melpomene having the lowest population size of ~0.002–0.004 on average.
source: For inbred individuals (chosen for sequencing to facilitate genome assembly) among our genomic data (H. melpomene, H. timareta, H. numata, and H. pardalinus; see Supplementary file 1a), θ estimates vary among chromosomes by orders of magnitude, with the inbred genome of H. melpomene having the lowest population size of ~0.002–0.004 on average.
evidence: This is an observation about parameter estimates for inbred individuals.

claim: Adding more individuals should help stabilize estimates of θ, but should not affect estimates of age or introgression rates.
source: Adding more individuals should help stabilize estimates of θ, but should not affect estimates of age or introgression rates.
evidence: This is a speculation about how sampling more individuals would affect parameter estimates.

claim: The introgression model of Figure 2B assumes that gene flow occurs in single pulses, which may be unrealistic if gene flow is ongoing.
source: The introgression model of Figure 2B assumes that gene flow occurs in single pulses. This may be unrealistic if gene flow is ongoing.
evidence: This is a statement about a modeling assumption and its potential limitation.

claim: The MSC-M model assumes continuous gene flow since lineage divergence at the rate of M migrants per generation.
source: The MSC-M model assumes continuous gene flow since lineage divergence at the rate of M migrants per generation (Flouri et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a description of the MSC-M model with a citation.

claim: The results under the MSC-M model concur with the introgression pulse model in suggesting high gene flow between H. pardalinus and H. elevatus.
source: The results concur with the introgression pulse model in suggesting high gene flow between H. pardalinus and H. elevatus (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A and B, Supplementary file 1s).
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-M analysis.

claim: There is evidence of gene flow between H. hecale and H. pardalinus/H. elevatus at lower levels, with M < 0.1 in most chromosomes.
source: There is also evidence of gene flow between H. hecale and H. pardalinus/H. elevatus at lower levels, with M < 0.1 in most chromosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A, Supplementary file 1s).
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-M analysis.

claim: Allowing for continuous gene flow as well as gene flow involving H. hecale results in slightly older estimates of both species divergence times (between H. pardalinus and H. elevatus, and between H. hecale and H. pardalinus + H. elevatus) than under the single-pulse introgression model.
source: Allowing for continuous gene flow as well as gene flow involving H. hecale, we obtain slightly older estimates of both species divergence times (between H. pardalinus and H. elevatus, and between H. hecale and H. pardalinus + H. elevatus) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A, Supplementary file 1s), than under the single-pulse introgression model (Supplementary file 1q and r).
evidence: This is a comparison of parameter estimates between models.

claim: The cydno-melpomene clade shows a similar pattern of older divergence times with substantial gene flow between all three species although at smaller magnitudes (M ~0.01–0.1).
source: The cydno-melpomene clade shows a similar pattern of older divergence times with substantial gene flow between all three species although at smaller magnitudes (M ~0.01–0.1) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C, Supplementary file 1u).
evidence: This is a finding from the MSC-M analysis.

claim: A model with continuous gene flow involving all three species may better describe the history of both the pardalinus-hecale clade and the cydno-melpomene clade.
source: We conclude that a model with continuous gene flow involving all three species may better describe the history of both the pardalinus-hecale clade and the cydno-melpomene clade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the MSC-I and MSC-M results.

claim: Substantial gene flow within the cydno-melpomene and pardalinus-hecale clades was identified based on both pulse introgression (MSC-I) and continuous migration (MSC-M) models.
source: In summary, we have identified substantial gene flow within the cydno-melpomene and pardalinus-hecale clades based on both pulse introgression (MSC-I) and continuous migration (MSC-M) models (Figure 2C and D,, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Supplementary file 1q–u).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analysis.

claim: Earlier genomic studies failed to quantify the intensity of gene flow (introgression probability or migration rate) or infer direction and timing of gene flow.
source: Earlier genomic studies failed to quantify the intensity of gene flow (introgression probability or migration rate) or infer direction and timing of gene flow.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work.

claim: Gene flow within the cydno-melpomene clade has been extensively studied at population/subspecies levels and at specific loci involved in wing pattern mimicry.
source: Gene flow within the cydno-melpomene clade has been extensively studied at population/subspecies levels and at specific loci involved in wing pattern mimicry (Bull et al., 2006; Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Kronforst et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2013; Wallbank et al., 2016; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2019), but gene flow involving other species has received less attention (Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Wallbank et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Jay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work with citations.

claim: Gene flow involving other species in the melpomene-silvaniform clade has received less attention.
source: Gene flow within the cydno-melpomene clade has been extensively studied at population/subspecies levels and at specific loci involved in wing pattern mimicry (Bull et al., 2006; Pardo-Diaz et al., 2012; Kronforst et al., 2013; Martin et al., 2013; Wallbank et al., 2016; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017; Martin et al., 2019), but gene flow involving other species has received less attention (Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Wallbank et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2016; Jay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work with citations.

claim: A polymorphic series of tandem inversions on chromosome 15 is involved in switching mimicry color pattern in H. numata.
source: A polymorphic series of tandem inversions on chromosome 15 is involved in switching mimicry color pattern in H. numata (Jay et al., 2018; Jay et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The first inversion, P1 (~400 kb), is in the 15b region (also called the P locus), and is fixed in H. pardalinus and retained as a polymorphism in H. numata.
source: The first inversion, P1 (~400 kb), is in the 15b region (also called the P locus), and is fixed in H. pardalinus and retained as a polymorphism in H. numata (Joron et al., 2011; Le Poul et al., 2014; Jay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Multiple introgression events are necessary to make the 15b tree compatible with either the Z chromosome tree or the autosomal trees, suggesting a much more complex introgression history of this region than in the rest of the genome.
source: Multiple introgression events are necessary to make the 15b tree (Figure 2A, scenario d, tree 24) compatible with either the Z chromosome tree or the autosomal trees (Figure 2A, scenarios a–c), suggesting a much more complex introgression history of this region than in the rest of the genome.
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic patterns.

claim: The 15b inversion contains the known wing patterning locus cortex, where it is maintained as a balanced polymorphism by natural selection.
source: This inversion contains the known wing patterning locus cortex (Jay et al., 2022), where it is maintained as a balanced polymorphism by natural selection (Joron et al., 2006; Nadeau et al., 2016; Van Belleghem et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Among the species without the inversion, the cydno-melpomene clade clusters with H. elevatus and is nested within the pardalinus-hecale clade (without H. pardalinus) in the 15b region.
source: Another feature of this 15b region is that among the species without the inversion, the cydno-melpomene clade clusters with H. elevatus and is nested within the pardalinus-hecale clade (without H. pardalinus).
evidence: This is a finding from the phylogenetic analysis of the 15b region.

claim: The pattern in the 15b region is contrary to the expectation based on the topologies in the rest of the genome that the cydno-melpomene clade would be sister to the pardalinus-hecale clade (without H. pardalinus).
source: This is contrary to the expectation based on the topologies in the rest of the genome (Figure 2A, scenarios a–c) that the cydno-melpomene clade would be sister to the pardalinus-hecale clade (without H. pardalinus).
evidence: This is an observation about the discrepancy between the 15b region and the rest of the genome.

claim: One explanation for the pattern in the 15b region is that introgression occurred between the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade and either H. elevatus or the common ancestor of H. elevatus and H. pardalinus together with a total replacement of the non-inverted 15b in H. pardalinus by the P1 inversion from H. numata.
source: One explanation for this pattern is that introgression occurred between the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade and either H. elevatus or the common ancestor of H. elevatus and H. pardalinus together with a total replacement of the non-inverted 15b in H. pardalinus by the P1 inversion from H. numata (Jay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation with a citation to prior work.

claim: The analysis confirms and quantifies the introgression in the 15b region.
source: We confirm and quantify this introgression below.
evidence: This is a statement about what the analysis accomplishes.

claim: Using data from additional species, a better resolution of species relationships along chromosome 15 was obtained, although with some uncertainty within the inversion region due to small numbers of loci.
source: Using data from additional species ('silv_chr15' dataset in Supplementary file 1a; see 'Methods'), we obtain a better resolution of species relationships along chromosome 15, although with some uncertainty within the inversion region due to small numbers of loci (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 1v).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of the expanded dataset.

claim: The analysis of independent data agrees with the Z chromosome tree and with (unrooted) trees obtained from concatenation analysis by Jay et al., 2018 and Jay et al., 2021, where H. numata with the inversion groups with H. pardalinus while H. numata without the inversion groups with its sister species, H. ismenius.
source: This analysis of independent data agrees with the Z chromosome tree (tree 24 in Figure 2A) and with (unrooted) trees obtained from concatenation analysis by Jay et al., 2018 (their Figures 2 and S1) and Jay et al., 2021 (their Figure S4), where H. numata with the inversion groups with H. pardalinus while H. numata without the inversion groups with its sister species, H. ismenius (Figure 3A, red trees).
evidence: This is a finding that agrees with prior work, with citations.

claim: Outside the inversion region, H. numata with both inversion genotypes groups with H. ismenius as expected.
source: Outside the inversion region, H. numata with both inversion genotypes groups with H. ismenius as expected (Figure 3A, blue trees).
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis.

claim: The sister relationship between H. numata and H. ismenius agrees with previous genomic studies of the autosomes and the sex chromosome.
source: Although this conclusion assumes that H. numata and H. ismenius are sister species while H. ismenius is not included in our species tree analysis of the melpomene-silvaniform clade (Figure 2), this sister relationship agrees with previous genomic studies of the autosomes and the sex chromosome (Zhang et al., 2016; Jay et al., 2021; Cicconardi et al., 2023; Rougemont et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: One parsimonious explanation is that the inversion originated either in H. numata after diverging from H. ismenius, or before the H. numata–H. ismenius split but was subsequently lost in H. ismenius, followed by introgression which introduced the inversion from H. numata into H. pardalinus, either before or after its divergence from H. elevatus.
source: Given that H. numata is an early-diverging lineage of the melpomene-silvaniform clade (Figure 2B) and is polymorphic for P1 over large parts of its geographic distribution while H. pardalinus is fixed for this inversion (Joron et al., 2011; Jay et al., 2022), one parsimonious explanation is that the inversion originated either in H. numata after diverging from H. ismenius, or before the H. numata–H. ismenius split but was subsequently lost in H. ismenius, followed by introgression which introduced the inversion from H. numata into H. pardalinus, either before or after its divergence from H. elevatus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on parsimony and prior knowledge, with citations.

claim: If the introgression occurred before H. pardalinus–H. elevatus divergence, the lack of the inversion in H. elevatus can be explained by another introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade into H. elevatus, completely replacing the inversion with the original orientation.
source: If the introgression occurred before H. pardalinus–H. elevatus divergence, the lack of the inversion in H. elevatus can be explained by another introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade into H. elevatus, completely replacing the inversion with the original orientation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the observed pattern.

claim: This introgression route (from the cydno-melpomene clade into H. elevatus) is reported in previous genomic studies, including at a different locus (optix gene, also involved in color pattern) in chromosome 18 as well as in the 15b region of chromosome 15.
source: This introgression route is reported in previous genomic studies, including at a different locus (optix gene, also involved in color pattern) in chromosome 18 as well as in the 15b region of chromosome 15 (Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Wallbank et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Under the scenario where the inversion originated in H. numata and introgressed into H. pardalinus, we might expect the 15b region to be less diverse in H. pardalinus (recipient of P1) than in H. numata (donor of P1), with the magnitude depending on the duration between the origin of P1 and introgression into H. pardalinus.
source: Under this scenario, we might expect the 15b region to be less diverse in H. pardalinus (recipient of P1) than in H. numata (donor of P1), with the magnitude depending on the duration between the origin of P1 and introgression into H. pardalinus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on population genetic theory.

claim: Reduced heterozygosity in H. pardalinus compared to H. numata is not seen in the data, suggesting that the transfer likely occurred early, shortly after the formation of the inversion in H. numata, or shortly after the H. numata–H. ismenius split if the inversion originated earlier.
source: However, we do not see this reduced heterozygosity in our data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the transfer likely occurred early, shortly after the formation of the inversion in H. numata, or shortly after the H. numata–H. ismenius split if the inversion originated earlier.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed heterozygosity data.

claim: The 15b tree having similar times of divergence between H. ismenius and H. numata without the inversion, and between H. pardalinus and H. numata with the inversion, further supports the scenario that the transfer occurred early.
source: This scenario is further supported by the 15b tree having similar times of divergence between H. ismenius and H. numata without the inversion, and between H. pardalinus and H. numata with the inversion (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference from the divergence time estimates.

claim: The topology of the 15b tree indicates that the first split is between species with the inversion (H. numata and H. pardalinus) and those without the inversion.
source: The topology of the 15b tree (Figures 2A and 3A) also indicates that the first split is between species with the inversion (H. numata and H. pardalinus) and those without the inversion.
evidence: This is an observation from the phylogenetic tree.

claim: Another possibility is that inversion polymorphism could have existed earlier in the history of the melpomene-silvaniform clade but was subsequently lost in most species.
source: This suggests another possibility: inversion polymorphism could have existed earlier in the history of the melpomene-silvaniform clade but was subsequently lost in most species (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a proposed alternative explanation.

claim: In the scenario of ancestral polymorphism, the ancestral polymorphism is maintained in H. numata while the inversion is fixed in H. pardalinus but is lost in other species.
source: In this scenario, the ancestral polymorphism is maintained in H. numata while the inversion is fixed in H. pardalinus but is lost in other species.
evidence: This describes the ancestral polymorphism scenario.

claim: Introgression between H. numata and H. pardalinus is not required under the ancestral polymorphism scenario but could still occur.
source: Introgression between H. numata and H. pardalinus is not required but could still occur.
evidence: This is a statement about the ancestral polymorphism scenario.

claim: Three additional bidirectional introgression events were added onto the main model in Figure 2B to reconcile the introgression history of 15b with the overall species tree.
source: To reconcile the introgression history of 15b with the overall species tree, we add three additional bidirectional introgression events onto the main model in Figure 2B and assess their plausibility using bpp.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: The results best support unidirectional introgression from H. numata into the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H. elevatus, and from the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade into H. elevatus shortly after its divergence from H. pardalinus.
source: Our results best support unidirectional introgression from H. numata into the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H. elevatus, and from the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade into H. elevatus shortly after its divergence from H. pardalinus (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, model m3).
evidence: This is a finding from the model comparison.

claim: In other scenarios, estimated introgression times tend to collapse onto the H. pardalinus–H elevatus divergence time, suggesting that the introgression events were likely misplaced.
source: In other scenarios, estimated introgression times tend to collapse onto the H. pardalinus–H elevatus divergence time, suggesting that the introgression events were likely misplaced (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1w).
evidence: This is an observation from the model fitting that suggests model misspecification.

claim: The finding that divergence of H. elevatus and introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade occurred almost simultaneously provides evidence for a hybrid speciation origin of H. elevatus resulting from introgression between H. pardalinus and the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade.
source: Our finding that divergence of H. elevatus and introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade occurred almost simultaneously provides evidence for a hybrid speciation origin of H. elevatus resulting from introgression between H. pardalinus and the common ancestor of the cydno-melpomene clade (Rosser et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference from the timing of divergence and introgression, with a citation to prior work.

claim: In an alternative scenario proposed by Jay et al., 2018, the inversion first originated in the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H elevatus, and subsequently introgressed into some subspecies of H. numata, while the inversion in H. elevatus was completely replaced by introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade.
source: In an alternative scenario proposed by Jay et al., 2018, the inversion first originated in the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H elevatus, and subsequently introgressed into some subspecies of H. numata, while the inversion in H. elevatus was completely replaced by introgression from the cydno-melpomene clade (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a description of an alternative scenario from prior work with a citation.

claim: Jay et al., 2018 used sliding-window gene tree topologies to support introgression of the inversion from H. pardalinus to H. numata shortly after its formation in the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H elevatus.
source: They used sliding-window gene tree topologies to support introgression of the inversion from H. pardalinus to H. numata shortly after its formation in the common ancestor of H. pardalinus and H elevatus (their Figures 4 and S4).
evidence: This is a description of the evidence used in prior work with a citation.

claim: By including H. ismenius and H. elevatus, sister species of H. numata and H. pardalinus, respectively, different directions of introgression should lead to different gene tree topologies.
source: By including H. ismenius and H. elevatus, sister species of H. numata and H. pardalinus, respectively, different directions of introgression should lead to different gene tree topologies.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about how gene tree topologies should differ depending on introgression direction.

claim: Tree topologies supporting each direction of introgression (H. numata → H. pardalinus versus H. pardalinus → H. numata) were almost equally common within the inversion region, particularly in the first half of the inversion, undermining the argument for a specific direction.
source: However, tree topologies supporting each direction of introgression were almost equally common within the inversion region, particularly in the first half of the inversion, undermining this argument.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis that contradicts the prior interpretation.

claim: With high levels of ILS and introgression in the group, estimated gene trees need not reflect the true species relationships.
source: With high levels of ILS and introgression in the group, estimated gene trees need not reflect the true species relationships.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of gene tree inference in the presence of ILS and introgression.

claim: Another variant of the alternative scenario is that the inversion originated in H. pardalinus after its divergence from H. elevatus and was introgressed into some subspecies of H. numata.
source: Another variant of this scenario is that the inversion originated in H. pardalinus after its divergence from H. elevatus and was introgressed into some subspecies of H. numata (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a description of another alternative scenario.

claim: The scenario where the inversion originated in H. pardalinus after its divergence from H. elevatus is considered unlikely because the inversion appears to have originated long before the H. pardalinus–H. elevatus split given deep divergence of lineages with and without the inversion.
source: We consider this scenario unlikely because the inversion appears to originated long before the H. pardalinus–H. elevatus split given deep divergence of lineages with and without the inversion (see 15b trees in Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: This is an inference from the phylogenetic data.

claim: The full-likelihood MSC approach yields several improvements over concatenation and other approximate methods for inferring species trees and introgression.
source: Our full-likelihood MSC approach yields several improvements over concatenation and other approximate methods for inferring species trees and introgression.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the advantages of the method.

claim: The MSC approach accounts for ILS due to coalescent fluctuations, so variation in inferred genealogical histories can be more firmly attributed to variation in gene flow across the genome.
source: First, we account for ILS due to coalescent fluctuations, so variation in inferred genealogical histories can be more firmly attributed to variation in gene flow across the genome.
evidence: This is a statement about an advantage of the method.

claim: The MSC approach analyzes the sequence data directly, rather than using estimated gene trees as data, which utilizes information in branch lengths of the gene trees while accommodating their uncertainty.
source: Second, we analyze the sequence data directly, rather than using estimated gene trees as data. This utilizes information in branch lengths of the gene trees while accommodating their uncertainty.
evidence: This is a statement about an advantage of the method.

claim: Heterozygous sites in the alignments were retained as unphased diploid sequences from each individual without collapsing them into a single randomly phased nucleotide.
source: We retain heterozygous sites in the alignments as unphased diploid sequences from each individual without collapsing them into a single randomly phased nucleotide as is common in other phylogenomic studies.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the data processing.

claim: The approach allows multiple individuals per species to be included, leading to improved estimation of introgression parameters.
source: Our approach allows multiple individuals per species to be included, leading to improved estimation of introgression parameters.
evidence: This is a statement about an advantage of the method.

claim: MSC models with pulse introgression (MSC-I) or continuous migration (MSC-M) allow direct estimation of key features of the direction, intensity, and timing of gene flow, and are applicable to gene flow between sister species.
source: Third, MSC models with pulse introgression (MSC-I) or continuous migration (MSC-M) allow direct estimation of key features of the direction, intensity, and timing of gene flow, and are applicable to gene flow between sister species.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the method.

claim: Widely used summary statistics such as D and fd do not estimate these parameters and cannot detect gene flow between sister lineages.
source: Widely used summary statistics such as D and fd do not estimate these parameters and cannot detect gene flow between sister lineages.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of approximate methods.

claim: Previous analyses using sliding-window concatenation or based on estimated gene trees were liable to be less successful for estimating branching order in the melpomene-silvaniform clade because they may be misled by rapid speciation events coupled with extensive gene flow.
source: Previous analyses using sliding-window concatenation or based on estimated gene trees were therefore liable to be less successful for estimating branching order in the melpomene-silvaniform clade, and because they may be misled by rapid speciation events coupled with extensive gene flow (Edelman et al., 2019; Massardo et al., 2020; Kozak et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior methods with citations.

claim: In the exploratory analysis of genomic blocks using MSC without gene flow, it is assumed that one of the main topologies represents the true species tree and is related to other topologies via introgression.
source: First, in the exploratory analysis of genomic blocks using MSC without gene flow (e.g. Figures 1A and 2A), we assume that one of the main topologies represents the true species tree and is related to other topologies via introgression.
evidence: This describes an assumption in the analytical approach.

claim: It can be nontrivial to decide which topology most likely represents the true species tree, and how to add introgression edges onto the assumed species tree to explain other topologies.
source: In general, it can be nontrivial to decide which topology most likely represents the true species tree, and how to add introgression edges onto the assumed species tree to explain other topologies.
evidence: This is a statement about a challenge in the analytical approach.

claim: Several strategies were employed including a recombination-rate argument, reduced introgression in the sex chromosome, estimates of pairwise migration rates under an explicit model of gene flow, and using additional evidence from geographic distributions and records of natural hybrids.
source: Here, we employ several strategies including a recombination-rate argument (Figure 1F), reduced introgression in the sex chromosome (Figure 2A), estimates of pairwise migration rates under an explicit model of gene flow (Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2), and using additional evidence from geographic distributions (Rosser et al., 2012) and records of natural hybrids (Mallet et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the strategies used to infer the true species tree.

claim: These strategies could fail in taxa with more limited biological or distribution information, or when the sex chromosome (if available) is less unreliable as to species topology.
source: These strategies could fail in taxa with more limited biological or distribution information, or when the sex chromosome (if available) is less unreliable as to species topology.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the strategies.

claim: Ideally, one would like to be able to estimate species phylogeny and introgression events simultaneously as part of a single unsupervised analysis, but this task remains computationally challenging.
source: Ideally, one would like to be able to estimate species phylogeny and introgression events simultaneously as part of a single unsupervised analysis, but this task remains computationally challenging.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of current methods.

claim: Software such as PhyloNet and starBEAST implement Bayesian inference of MSC with introgression but they are usually limited to small datasets of no more than 100 loci.
source: Software such as PhyloNet (Wen and Nakhleh, 2018) and starBEAST (Zhang et al., 2018) implement Bayesian inference of MSC with introgression but they are usually limited to small datasets of no more than 100 loci.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of existing software with citations.

claim: Heuristics based on summary statistics may attempt to place introgression edges onto a species phylogeny estimated on the assumption of no gene flow, but these approaches do not make full use of sequence data and can be misled by incorrect initial species trees.
source: Heuristics based on summary statistics may attempt to place introgression edges onto a species phylogeny estimated on the assumption of no gene flow (Malinsky et al., 2018; Suvorov et al., 2022; Cicconardi et al., 2023). However, these approaches do not make full use of sequence data and can be misled by incorrect initial species trees.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of approximate methods with citations.

claim: Approximate methods based on summary statistics cannot convincingly infer direction of gene flow or gene flow between sister species.
source: Furthermore, they cannot convincingly infer direction of gene flow or gene flow between sister species.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of approximate methods.

claim: Although the full-likelihood MSC approach is more powerful than approximate methods, it is also more computationally intensive and does not scale well to analyses of large numbers of species (>20, say).
source: Second, although our approach is more powerful than approximate methods, it is also more computationally intensive and does not scale well to analyses of large numbers of species (>20, say).
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the method.

claim: There are 47 species in six major clades in Heliconius.
source: In Heliconius, there are 47 species in six major clades.
evidence: This is a statement of taxonomic fact.

claim: The strategy has been to analyze subsets of species representing major clades or representative species within each clade, and then combine the results into a larger phylogeny.
source: Our strategy has therefore been to analyze subsets of species representing major clades or representative species within each clade. We then combine the results into a larger phylogeny.
evidence: This describes the analytical strategy used in the study.

claim: One caveat is that not all species get explored at the same time, and some introgression events may be missed.
source: One caveat is that not all species get explored at the same time, and some introgression events may be missed.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the analytical strategy.

claim: The MSC makes simplifying modeling assumptions such as neutral evolution, constant substitution rates on all branches, no recombination within each locus, and free recombination among loci.
source: Lastly, the MSC makes simplifying modeling assumptions such as neutral evolution, constant substitution rates on all branches, no recombination within each locus, and free recombination among loci, the implications of which have been discussed previously (Burgess and Yang, 2008; Thawornwattana et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a statement about the assumptions of the model with citations.

claim: Although the MSC model assumes constant rate neutral evolution, estimated introgression probabilities (φ) are a combination of both actual introgression and subsequent positive and negative selection on introgressed loci, the extent of which is modulated by local recombination rate.
source: We note that although the MSC model assumes constant rate neutral evolution, estimated introgression probabilities (φ) are a combination of both actual introgression and subsequent positive and negative selection on introgressed loci, the extent of which is modulated by local recombination rate (Petry, 1983; Barton and Bengtsson, 1986).
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of parameter estimates with citations.

claim: The approach first explores major species relationships across genome blocks using a full-likelihood MSC approach, then identifies introgression events that explain the different local species trees by proposing introgression edges on a background species topology.
source: In summary, we first explore major species relationships across genome blocks using a full-likelihood MSC approach. We then identify introgression events that explain the different local species trees by proposing introgression edges on a background species topology, with additional evidence from explicit models of gene flow.
evidence: This is a summary of the analytical approach.

claim: Geographic distributions and the prevalence of natural hybrids can be employed to help with placement of introgression edges in a phylogeny.
source: In addition, geographic distributions and the prevalence of natural hybrids can be employed to help with placement of introgression edges in a phylogeny.
evidence: This describes additional information used in the analysis.

claim: This process can result in several competing introgression models, which are then evaluated by estimating parameters under each model using sequence data, evaluating the model fit, and performing model comparison.
source: This process can result in several competing introgression models. We estimate parameters under each model using sequence data, evaluate the model fit, and perform model comparison.
evidence: This describes the model comparison approach.

claim: By breaking the problem into manageable parts, the approach is computationally tractable.
source: By breaking the problem into manageable parts in this way, our approach is computationally tractable.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational feasibility of the approach.

claim: Phylogenetic relationships among major clades within Heliconius were clarified and major introgression events were quantified, including introgression between sister species.
source: We have clarified phylogenetic relationships among major clades within Heliconius and quantified major introgression events, including introgression between sister species (which does not change tree topology).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings.

claim: Within the melpomene-silvaniform clade, a robust pattern was obtained in which the common ancestor of H. besckei, H. numata, and H. ismenius first split off from the rest, rendering the silvaniform species paraphyletic.
source: Second, within the melpomene-silvaniform clade, we obtained a robust pattern in which the common ancestor of H. besckei, H. numata, and H. ismenius first split off from the rest, rendering the silvaniform species paraphyletic (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding.

claim: The finding that silvaniforms are paraphyletic is contrary to a common belief that the silvaniforms are monophyletic.
source: This is contrary to a common belief that the silvaniforms are monophyletic (Heliconius Genome Consortium, 2012; Kozak et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2021; Kozak et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior beliefs with citations.

claim: The P1 inversion on chromosome 15 involved in wing pattern mimicry likely introgressed from H. numata into H. pardalinus based on species tree topologies and direct modeling of introgression.
source: Third, the P1 inversion on chromosome 15 involved in wing pattern mimicry likely introgressed from H. numata into H. pardalinus based on species tree topologies (Figures 2 and 3) and direct modeling of introgression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), although where and when it originated remain uncertain.
evidence: This is a summary of a key finding with some uncertainty.

claim: The P1 inversion likely arose in H. numata or its close ancestor and became fixed in H. pardalinus via an introgression replacement event from the former species, although a deeper origin followed by persistent ancestral polymorphism remains a possibility.
source: Overall, we conclude that the P1 inversion likely arose in H. numata or its close ancestor and became fixed in H. pardalinus via an introgression replacement event from the former species (Figure 3B), although a deeper origin followed by persistent ancestral polymorphism (Figure 3C) remains a possibility.
evidence: This is a conclusion with some uncertainty.

claim: Heliconius is an example of recent and rapid diversification with extensive gene flow occurring between closely related species as well as between more divergent lineages throughout its history at varying degrees.
source: Heliconius is an example of recent and rapid diversification with extensive gene flow occurring between closely related species as well as between more divergent lineages throughout its history at varying degrees.
evidence: This is a characterization of the evolutionary history of Heliconius.

claim: Since many species pairs of Heliconius show high degrees of sympatry today, there are plenty of opportunities for low levels of gene flow to occur whenever their ranges overlap.
source: Since many species pairs of Heliconius show high degrees of sympatry today, there are plenty of opportunities for low levels of gene flow to occur whenever their ranges overlap (Rosser et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference about opportunities for gene flow with a citation.

claim: This fact is evident in the estimates of pairwise migration rates among species in the melpomene-silvaniform clade.
source: This fact is evident in our estimates of pairwise migration rates among species in the melpomene-silvaniform clade (Appendix 1—figures 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a reference to findings in the appendix.

claim: There are many documented natural hybrids and there is evidence for introgression between particular pairs of subspecies from genomic studies, most of which involve wing patterning loci.
source: There are many documented natural hybrids (Mallet et al., 2007) and there is evidence for introgression between particular pairs of subspecies from genomic studies, most of which involve wing patterning loci (Wallbank et al., 2016; Enciso-Romero et al., 2017; Morris et al., 2020; Rougemont et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study did not attempt to incorporate all possible introgression signals into the phylogeny but instead focused on major introgression events that explain major patterns of species tree variation across the genome using a representative subset of species.
source: We did not attempt to incorporate all possible introgression signals into our phylogeny but instead focused on major introgression events that explain major patterns of species tree variation across the genome using a representative subset of species.
evidence: This describes the scope of the analysis.

claim: The phylogeny in Figure 4 should be viewed as a simplified version of reality.
source: Thus our phylogeny in Figure 4 should be viewed as a simplified version of reality.
evidence: This is a caveat about the interpretation of the phylogeny.

claim: One future direction is to model a low level of admixture among all lineages.
source: One future direction is to model a low level of admixture among all lineages.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work.

claim: The phylogeny indicates that the aoede clade, comprising H. aoede and three other species, is likely the earliest-branching lineage of Heliconius, followed by the erato-sara clade.
source: Our phylogeny indicates that the aoede clade, comprising H. aoede and three other species, is likely the earliest-branching lineage of Heliconius, followed by the erato-sara clade.
evidence: This is a summary of a key phylogenetic finding.

claim: This branching order is consistent with a phylogeny based on morphological and behavioral characters.
source: This branching order is consistent with a phylogeny based on morphological and behavioral characters (Penz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Since the aoede clade is the only group of Heliconius that does not feed on pollen, the aoede-early scenario suggests that unique pollen feeding traits arose once after the divergence of the aoede clade.
source: Since the aoede clade is the only group of Heliconius that does not feed on pollen (Brown, 1981), the aoede-early scenario (Figure 1C) suggests that unique pollen feeding traits arose once after the divergence of the aoede clade (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference about trait evolution based on the phylogeny, with a citation.

claim: In contrast, the erato-early scenario is less parsimonious as it requires an additional loss of pollen feeding ability in the aoede clade.
source: In contrast, the erato-early scenario (Figure 1B) is less parsimonious as it requires an additional loss of pollen feeding ability in the aoede clade (Cicconardi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is an inference about parsimony with a citation.

claim: Turner, 1976 named the aoede clade as subgenus Neruda based on distinct morphology in all life stages.
source: Turner, 1976 named the aoede clade as subgenus Neruda based on distinct morphology in all life stages, such as pupae that are more similar to those of Eueides (a sister genus of Heliconius), unique larva morphology, white eggs like those of Eueides (instead of yellow eggs in all other Heliconius), a different genus of larval host plant, Dilkea (Benson et al., 1975) (all other Heliconius species feed on Passiflora), and chromosome numbers of n = 21–31 which are variable and intermediate between Heliconius (n = 21 in most species) and Eueides (n = 31) (Brown et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Brown, 1981 later raised Neruda from subgenus to genus.
source: For these reasons, Brown, 1981 later raised Neruda from subgenus to genus.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Morphological/behavioral/ecological characters tend to support early divergence of the aoede clade.
source: Thus, morphological/behavioral/ecological characters tend to support early divergence of the aoede clade (Brown, 1972; Penz, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Molecular phylogenetic work seemed to support the erato-early scenario.
source: Molecular phylogenetic work, on the other hand, seemed to support the erato-early scenario (Figure 1B; Brower and Egan, 1997; Beltrán et al., 2007; Kozak et al., 2015; Kozak et al., 2021; Cicconardi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Consequently, generic status of Neruda was revoked.
source: Consequently, generic status of Neruda was revoked (Kozak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The full-likelihood approach, which accounts for ILS as well as introgression, enables inference of a phylogeny that is more parsimonious with morphology and life history.
source: Our full-likelihood approach, which accounts for ILS as well as introgression, enables inference of a phylogeny that is more parsimonious with morphology and life history.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the advantage of the method.

claim: This result parallels analysis of genomic data from African mosquitoes in the Anopheles gambiae species complex, in which coalescent-based likelihood analyses support species trees that are more parsimonious for chromosomal rearrangement data, while prior sliding-window and concatenation analysis favored trees that are less parsimonious.
source: This result parallels analysis of genomic data from African mosquitoes in the Anopheles gambiae species complex, in which coalescent-based likelihood analyses support species trees that are more parsimonious for chromosomal rearrangement data (Thawornwattana et al., 2018), while prior sliding-window and concatenation analysis favored trees that are less parsimonious (Fontaine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with prior work with citations.

claim: The likelihood analyses can be used to rescue generic or subgeneric status for Neruda.
source: Our likelihood analyses can thus be used to rescue generic or subgeneric status for Neruda.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the taxonomic implications of the findings.

claim: There remains considerable uncertainty near the base of Heliconius.
source: Nevertheless, there remains considerable uncertainty near the base of Heliconius.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the findings.

claim: Further whole-genome data from H. aoede and related species in the aoede, burneyi and doris clades will likely improve resolution.
source: Further whole-genome data from H. aoede and related species in the aoede, burneyi and doris clades will likely improve resolution.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work.
